Dear Akun heeded
The discerning judge's words,
And gave the fierce woman
As a bride to Khan Manas.
She was the khan's wife;
Now she was an ill-fated bondwoman,
Her head seized as spoil—
The very accursed woman.
For this graceful woman,
This grievous infidel woman,
This woman grown old,
There could be no place among the people
Of these people-wearing infidels.
Look at the way she moves!
She was the wife of a hero blessed by Khydyr;
Her calamity will touch many.
Her son is famed as Khan Semetey.
Will this bloody clan bow
And submit to another?
If she does not die, this woman's conflict
Will fall upon the Zhediger.
Will princely, gray-maned Semetey
Allow another to tread his bed?
Will he not strike from above?
Will anyone who treads the pillow
Of the famed hero, the Magnanimous One, prosper?
This evil deed, this disastrous affair—
Will it not strike us to the soul?
Hearing Kanchoro had spoken thus,
Dear Kiyaz grew agitated.
He had come to take a wife
And met with great turmoil.
Kanchoro turned blood into blood
And laid the bloodthirsty hero low.
Finding no place to flee,
Finding no deep pit to enter,
Will we die a wretched death?
With the people ruined and the nation fleeing,
Will we die a wretched death?
The wise men said these things;
Some souls whispered,
Listening to one another
And probing what lay behind the words.
They nudged one another in the ribs
And trembled together.
Some wise men among the Zhediger
Had begun to judge the matter.
Thinking of what would follow, some
Had entered into dispute.
Some witless men,
Excited after eating at the feast,
Said, "We have taken a woman as spoil,"
And reveled in their own thoughts.
"What will become of our precious days?" they wondered.
Many noble men pondered this.
"Saying we would take a wife and live in ease,
How many people have we killed?"
Foolish men pondered this.
Across the plain of Jeti-Kyr,
At accomplished Kiyaz's wedding,
Plane trees ringed the place,
With a golden throne at the center.
From the tower, the people's landmark,
A herald shouted.
Hero Kiyaz, son of Bagysh,
Had a decree proclaimed to the people.
Ready as a hawk,
Having devised a cunning plan,
The multitude of Zhediger
Heard the khan's decree was coming:
He would give the masses
A great wedding feast for taking a wife;
Now that the prince had taken a wife,
He would scatter all four kinds of livestock.
Without binding ropes or blindfolding eyes,
He would open a spectacle
To astound the multitude;
Wrestlers would seize each other's cuffs,
Come forth and grapple,
And stage a spectacle.
The poles would bend;
In this extraordinary affair,
Champion warriors would joust.
Then hero Kiyaz
Made a proclamation to the multitude.
Dear Kiyaz shouted,
Calling the Zhediger:
"Come, every one of you, leave none behind!
Damn your fathers' graves, Zhediger!
Call it Khan Kiyaz's design;
Call it the wedding feast
Of the noble, unfortunate beauty Aichurok.
Do you know, Zhediger?
From your broad, level Kyzan,
I have brought my migration.
For the hero consumed by longing for Churok,
I sit here taking vengeance.
The banks of Zhylgyndy, Keng-Kol, and Talas
I have taken and now possess.
For the two khans Chynkojo and Toltoy,
I sit here taking vengeance.
Making the earth marvel
And call me Kiyaz the hero,
I have won her and sit here.
The noble peri Aichurok,
That radiant, unfortunate woman,
I have taken as my wife.
The gold and silver
Of gray-maned Semetey, Manas's son,
I have loaded and brought home.
The thimble mouth and dark eyes,
The great shining camel-calf eyes,
The crimson dress and moon-slender waist,
The graceful beauty—
I have seized and brought her here.
Rejoicing in the strength that seized her,
I shall hold a feast for many peoples.
If I rise against the whole world,
I intend to overthrow it.
I am your lord and your lion,
Your gray-maned hero Kiyaz!
At the gray wolf's words,
Multitudes of Zhediger,
Your champions and your khans,
Lose yourselves in the spectacle;
Let every one of you plunge into the fray!
Now that I have taken the noble peri,
I have openly held a feast for my people;
I have conceived a design beyond mankind.
I shall begin many wonders;
For moonlike Lady Churok,
Not only my livestock, but my very life—
I shall utterly give it all away.
For this woman's wedding,
I shall stake a yellow velvet fur coat;
I shall stake livestock in tens of thousands.
Instead of one, I shall stake a thousand;
I shall stake a camel that carries gold.
I shall stake splendid livestock;
As prizes for you, multitude,
I shall stake red-tailed riding camels.
I shall quickly stake my wealth;
Thousands of horses with fathom-long tails,
Mounts for champions, I shall stake.
If these prizes are too little,
Stake all the myriad Zhediger people!
If they do not suffice, I shall stake giants.
Without breaking up the herds on pasture,
I have staked all the abundant livestock.
Let wrestlers grapple and heroes joust;
Let there be lung-fighting and bald men's contests.
Let the spectacle surpass all others.
When the people depart roaring with laughter,
Is this not the mark of khanship?
Is this not the deed
Of a mighty, sacred soul?
To govern the people and know the nation—
Is this not the mark of khanship?
To wear a bare sword at one's side—
Is this not lordly power?
To govern the people and sustain the realm—
Come, my people, is this not lordly power?
For Lady Churok's wedding,
I shall spend all my strength,
Lavish all my countless wealth,
And scatter everything I possess.
Long ago, beside the waters of Jeti-Ozon,
At the wedding where Kiyaz took a wife,
At the feast he gave the people,
Let them say, 'Such was the skill displayed,
And thus his country encamped.'
Let the populace clamor and speak of it;
To every soul who hears, may this feast
Sit as smoothly as butter.
Let the victor become rich;
Let the fallen remain empty-handed.
Let them say, 'Such was the skill,
Such was the example,
Such was the gracious khan's design,
Such was the pattern;
Such was the great clamor he gave the people,
Such was their entertainment.'
Tell what you saw
To old men sunk into their beds,
And to stumbling children
Who have not yet gathered their wits.
Let the people bustle and raise a din;
Rejoice, my people,
For the dear lady's wedding.
For this unfortunate noble peri,
How could I spare my livestock?
Not merely my livestock—for Churok,
How could I spare my life?
If these prizes are too little,
Stake the mighty winged steed,
My horse Tootoru;
Stake a land like Jeti-Ozon.
If these prizes are to be opened,
Stake the people, beginning with the Zhediger!
At such a splendid, great wedding,
Would stinginess bring any good?
Will one who withholds a gracious word
Ever prosper?
When their khan issued his decree,
The old men grew excited;
As though massacre had struck,
Every one of them grew excited.
"The khan's decree has come;
He ordered, 'Let none remain behind,'"
They said, and two men seized each camel by the tusks,
Making their great teeth jut out,
Their lower lips sag,
Their necks rise like ducks',
Their two humps bulge,
Their long hair trail—
A sight to gladden the soul.
Nursing secret resentment and pressing on,
So the bald men might win the prize,
Hero Kiyaz's attendants
Led a thousand riding camels,
Urging them forward with cries.
Hero Kiyaz's attendants
To add to the prize
Led a thousand dark blaze-faced mares.
In the great arena amid the people,
A herald stood upon the tower.
A wrestler came and struck
The great drum that summoned the people.
Black Taz of Kapchalchi
Came out to clash;
Yellow Taz, the judge's son,
Came out to fight him.
Taking lungs in their hands,
Barefoot and bareheaded,
The two bald-pated paupers—
When those two madmen fought,
The people who saw them drew back.
Their two heads shone
As though moonlight struck them, making people laugh.
They staked a great prize
And fought with raw lungs.
The stronger pounded the weaker
Until his strength was gone;
They made a marvelous spectacle.
If you looked upon the great games,
Heroes and wrestlers seized each other's cuffs,
Clashed with one another,
Butted like gray bulls,
And tore at each other like hungry stallion-camels.
Like hungry wolves,
They mauled whatever part they reached.
One of these wrestlers
Had lived in the bloodthirsty leopard's house;
There was a great sorcerer there,
